title: Joule's Law, Electric Power, Bulb Ratings, kWh, and Temperature Coefficient of Resistance

claims.text: Joule's law of heating: current flowing through a resistor converts electrical energy into heat. Derivation: for charge dQ moved across potential difference V in time dt, work done dW=V dQ=VI dt (using I=dQ/dt). Total work in time t: W = integral(VI dt) = VIt (for constant V, I). Using V=IR, this heat energy can also be written W = I^2 R t = V^2 t / R
Electric power P is the rate of energy dissipation: P = W/t = VI = I^2 R = V^2/R. SI unit: watt (W) = joule/second; 1 W = 1 J/1 s

Bulb rating numerical: a bulb rated 220 V, 60 W (or 20 W in the specific worked example) consumes that many joules of energy per second when connected across 220 V. Maximum permissible current through the bulb: I=P/V (e.g. for 20W/220V, I=1/11 A). Filament resistance: from P=V^2/R, R=V^2/P (e.g. R=220x220/20 ohm)

Electrical energy is commercially measured in kilowatt-hour (kWh, the 'unit' on an electricity bill), not joules: energy = power x time, with power in kilowatts and time in hours. 1 kWh is the energy consumed by an appliance rated 1 kW running for 1 hour. Conversion: 1 kWh = 1000 W x 3600 s = 3.6x10^6 J

Temperature coefficient of resistance (alpha): defined via DeltaR proportional to R*DeltaT, i.e. alpha = DeltaR/(R DeltaT) = (Rt-R0)/(R0 DeltaT), giving Rt = R0(1+alpha*DeltaT). An exactly analogous temperature coefficient of resistivity (rho) is defined the same way: rho_t = rho_0(1+alpha*DeltaT). This mirrors the general pattern of linear/area/volume thermal expansion coefficients (alpha=DeltaL/(L0 DeltaT), beta=DeltaA/(A0 DeltaT), gamma=DeltaV/(V0 DeltaT), with alpha:beta:gamma = 1:2:3)

Resistivity vs temperature behaviour by material class: (a) METALS -- alpha is positive and comparatively large; resistivity rises with increasing temperature (rho-vs-T curve slopes upward). (b) SEMICONDUCTORS -- alpha is negative; resistivity FALLS as temperature rises (rho-vs-T curve slopes downward, since more charge carriers become available at higher temperature). (c) ALLOYS (e.g. manganin, constantan, nichrome) -- alpha is very small, i.e. resistance is nearly independent of temperature, which is exactly why these materials are chosen for precision resistors and heating elements

markdown_body:
## Joule's law of heating (NCERT 3.9)

Current through a resistor converts electrical energy into heat. For charge $dQ$ moved across potential difference $V$ in time $dt$: $dW = V\,dQ = VI\,dt$. Total work (constant $V,I$) over time $t$:
$$W = \int VI\,dt = VIt$$
Using $V=IR$, this heat can also be written:
$$W = I^2Rt = \frac{V^2}{R}t$$

## Electric power (NCERT 3.9)

$$P = \frac{W}{t} = VI = I^2R = \frac{V^2}{R}$$
SI unit: **watt** (W) $=$ J/s.

### Bulb rating numerical
A bulb rated $220$ V, (worked example: $20$ W) consumes that many joules per second at $220$ V.
- **Max permissible current:** $I = P/V$ (e.g. $20/220 = 1/11$ A)
- **Filament resistance:** from $P=V^2/R$, $R = V^2/P$ (e.g. $220\times220/20\ \Omega$)

### Kilowatt-hour
Electricity bills measure energy in **kilowatt-hours (kWh)**, not joules: energy $=$ power (kW) $\times$ time (h). $1$ kWh is the energy an appliance rated $1$ kW consumes running for $1$ hour:
$$1~\text{kWh} = 1000~\text{W}\times3600~\text{s} = 3.6\times10^6~\text{J}$$

## Temperature coefficient of resistance (NCERT 3.8)

$$\Delta R \propto R\,\Delta T \;\Rightarrow\; \alpha = \frac{\Delta R}{R\,\Delta T} = \frac{R_t-R_0}{R_0\,\Delta T} \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{R_t = R_0(1+\alpha\,\Delta T)}$$
The same relation holds for resistivity $\rho$: $\rho_t=\rho_0(1+\alpha\,\Delta T)$. (This mirrors the general pattern for thermal expansion coefficients: $\alpha=\Delta L/L_0\Delta T$, $\beta=\Delta A/A_0\Delta T$, $\gamma=\Delta V/V_0\Delta T$, with $\alpha:\beta:\gamma=1:2:3$.)

### By material class
- **Metals:** $\alpha$ positive, comparatively large — resistivity **rises** with temperature.
- **Semiconductors:** $\alpha$ **negative** — resistivity **falls** as temperature rises (more charge carriers become available at higher $T$).
- **Alloys** (manganin, constantan, nichrome): $\alpha$ very small — resistance is nearly temperature-independent, which is exactly why these are the materials chosen for precision resistors and heating elements.
